segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kendra and her husband and their two kids moved back to Boston, and it wasn't going great for her. She's a teacher but hadn't found a teaching job yet, so she did odd jobs-- a little thing at the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library. She worked as an usher for the Boston Symphony Orchestra, which-- can I say-- these are like the kind of Boston-specific jobs you would give a character who moved to Boston in a bad movie.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: Like, the only thing I wasn't doing is, like, selling foam "fingahs" at Fenway "Pahk."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: And I made, like, very little money.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She was actually pretty depressed, just dragging herself through the motions of living, not looking forward to anything. And it wouldn't go away. She couldn't shake it.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I would wake up in the morning and feel sort of irritated, like, oh, this again? I went to work, and I would have put a smile on my face, but I oftentimes would not hear anything anyone said to me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So she's four months into this new downer of a life, and she gets off work. And it's April, one of the first bright, sunny days after a long, dark winter. And she's excited to take her dog Schuyler to Wollaston Beach near her house on this pretty day. Wollaston's good for a dog, she says, because she's big and kind of a maniac.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: And so this beach is perfect because, really, no one was out. We started walking. I let her off leash, because she really wanted to splash around. And she was just frolicking. And I saw her moving closer to the water, and I realized my feet were starting to sink.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, wait. What do you mean "sink"?

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: Sure. So my one foot started to really sink, and then I was attempting to pull that foot out, and then my other foot started to sink. And I realized I was not hitting a hard bottom.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: So there was no one to call or cry. And it was really happening fast. I was really sinking quite fast. And I should note, Ira, like, I'm not a tall woman. I'm a 4 foot 10" woman. So for me to start sinking, like-- (LAUGHING) I was, like, practically up to my thighs in this muddy, sandy, watery mixture very quickly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Very quickly, like how quick?

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I would say maybe the whole, like, gravitational pull down into the sand was 30 seconds. It could have been three minutes, for all I know, because time just slowed down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As she struggled to yank her feet up, she realized the mud and sand and water formed a kind of seal around her boot, holding it down, making it too heavy to lift. And so scary, right? She thought to herself, am I about to break a bone, pulling my leg out? Am I trapped? Am I just going to keep sinking?

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I had no idea what to be afraid of. I just know that I was very afraid.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did you think that you could sink all the way under and just go all the way down?

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: Oh, yes. That's 100% where I thought I was headed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Quicksand, she thought. I'm in quicksand-- in Massachusetts. And I thought this was interesting. Apparently, when you find yourself sinking in quicksand, not on a tropical island or a jungle, not when you're poking around some ancient ruins, raiding the lost tombs of dead pharaohs in an old movie, but when it happens just like a 10-minute drive from your own house on a beach in Quincy, Massachusetts, nine minutes from one Dunkin' Donuts and eight minutes from another, the thought that inevitably goes through your head in that situation is, seriously?

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I said, this is bullshit. This is New England. Like, you're telling me that-- like, quicksand? Like, that's something out of Princess Bride. What is it doing at Wollaston Beach? And why aren't there signs to warn me about this?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. There's a bit that John Mulaney does-- the comedian John Mulaney-- that when I saw it, I felt like he was saying out loud something that I have always felt. He said that, based on what he saw on TV as a kid, he thought quicksand was going to be a much bigger part of his adulthood than it actually turned out to be.

segments.speaker: John Mulaney
segments.text: Because if you watch cartoons, quicksand is the third-biggest thing you have to worry about in adult life, behind real sticks of dynamite and giant anvils falling on you from the sky. Now I've gotten older, not only have I never stepped in quicksand, I've never even heard about it.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I also was thinking about John Mulaney.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You knew that bit?

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: Oh, John Mulaney is-- he's on heavy rotation with my kids and me. And I remember thinking, eat your heart out, John Mulaney. If you could see me now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so here she was, first up to our ankles, then her knees, now up to her thighs, and still sinking. Her cell phone was in the car. The beach was deserted, except for her dog, who was romping around happily like a goddamn idiot. No one to save her or help out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then this thing happened. Kendra says she's somebody who usually has a hard time expressing it when she's angry. She's somebody who cries rather than yells. But now, this wave of pure rage shot through her-- rage and outrage just erupting.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I was so pissed. Like, you know what? Like, I can't freaking believe this is how my day is going to go. Like, kick me while I'm down.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: Like, I was like, oh, hell, no, you are not going to ruin my day, sand. Like, I have fought for this lovely spring day. I am not going down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And with that burst of Hulk-like fury, she moves into action. She's like, quicksand? No problem. I will embrace the ridiculous awfulness of the situation, and I will make something happen right now. And she starts squirming around this way and that.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I started to lean backwards. And at that point, when I leaned back, I was still sinking, but I was hoping that I could sort of just wiggle out of my boots and that my boots would be the sort of sacrificial lamb that I would just leave in the sand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: But I realized, if I just leaned back and kind of shimmied like a drunk person getting onto a bar stool, I could lift my legs out of the sand, little by little by little. The only sort of impediment was that my dog was looking at me like, this is a fun game. I just don't know how to play it. Like, she was just kind of darting around me, watching me move like this. So then I was getting really, really frustrated with her as well.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She wiggled her way out onto solid ground. At that point, she says, she's completely covered in sand-- wet sand in her hair, all over her clothes. She collects her dog, climbs in her car, drives home, cleans up. A week or two passes, and then one morning, she wakes up and realizes she feels OK.

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: I remember so clearly, sitting in bed and saying to my husband, oh, my goodness. I think I'm good. I was filled with this content feeling that I can only describe as, like, the depression fading. Like, I didn't feel any of the heaviness. And I could only trace its disappearance to the quicksand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kendra thinks it has something to do with the anger she tapped into when she was stuck in the sand. As somebody who can't always express her anger, she thinks letting herself get so furious for once, it flipped something in her. That's the moment she was able to embrace just how bad things had gotten and fight her way out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, we have other stories of people put in difficult, sometimes impossible situations, and the only way out is to put their arms around the badness and feel it for what it is and then figure out some moves to wrestle the problem to the ground. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, Haley Mary Pass. It is the most magical week in American politics right now. Yes, it is. I'm speaking to you right now during the eight days between the Iowa caucus and the New Hampshire primary.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The way it works-- the results in Iowa will reset the political scores and possibilities, redeal all the cards. And so this week that we are in right now can be an enchanted eight days where underdogs tell themselves that anything is possible, anything can happen, no matter how unlikely it is to, in fact, happen. And to witness this in person, one of our producers, Zoe Chace, went to New Hampshire this week to hang out with two people, two old friends who've chosen to embrace hope in the face of long and difficult odds.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They know very well that Donald Trump will probably be the Republican nominee for president. And they are not happy about it. These guys are Democrats. But they are embracing the likelihood of Donald Trump's rise with a giant bear hug, and they are trying to do something about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they are making a last stand to try to stop him this very week. And basically, what they're trying to do is they're trying to convince New Hampshire voters to get real about their options in this historic moment and vote not for who they actually want to be president, but vote for the only person these guys believe can stop Donald Trump from becoming the Republican nominee. And that person is Nikki Haley.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's right. These two Democrats are stumping day and night to elect a woman who stands for so many things they personally hate. Zoe caught up with them one day before this enchanted week began-- that is a day before the Iowa caucus.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: These guys aren't even from New Hampshire. They're policy wonks from out of state, outside agitators. One's from DC, and the other's from New York. They both work for do-goodery, international-interest-type places they prefer not to name on the radio. Robert Schwartz has been living in New Hampshire for three months.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He took a leave from his job, left his family, moved up here with his good friend Kenny-- Ken Scheffler, friends from college. I met up with them at a brewery in Keene, New Hampshire. And they're here this particular afternoon because a politician is on stage-- someone running in the Democratic primary, which is happening, even though Joe Biden decided to skip New Hampshire this year.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The guy on stage, Congressman Dean Phillips, is making a random run for the presidency. But Robert and Ken are not paying attention to Dean Phillips. They're here for the 40 or 50 voters in the room. Robert is sort of irrepressible, says all his thoughts as he has them kind of thing, and starts whispering to me as soon as I get there.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Because a lot of the people here, I think they-- a lot of people haven't really made up their mind yet. And so it's good for us to be here and just talk to them, because it is a lot of people that are undeclared voters.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The way it works in New Hampshire, independent voters can vote in either primary-- Democrat or Republican. And there's a ton of people like that, something like 40% of the electorate. And this year, with Joe Biden skipping New Hampshire, Robert and Ken's mission is more plausible.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: All these people who probably would have voted for Biden are free agents. Robert and Ken are here to pick off some of those people-- Democratic-leaning independent voters who might be willing to vote for Nikki Haley as a way to stop Trump.

segments.speaker: Dean Phillips
segments.text: I love you all.

segments.speaker: Dean Phillips
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: As soon as the event ends, Robert walks up to a random voter he doesn't know anything about, who's someone all bundled up in a blue parka, to see if he can convince her to cast a vote against everything she just heard on stage and throw in with the Republican primary instead. He has a very slow roll-up.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Just what brings you-- I'm just curious, what brings you to this event?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, I want to see a change in the presidency. I don't like either one of them. Because Biden is too old, and I certainly don't want Donald Trump.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: You don't. And are you a registered Democrat or undeclared?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm independent, purposely.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Boom. He's found his target-- independent voter, leans to the left. You'd think he'd make his pitch. But he's learned this kind of voter doesn't like it when you open with a hard sell on Nikki Haley, because they don't like Nikki Haley, and he doesn't like Haley either. But he has to sell her on Haley, so it's kind of a weird conversation-- a lot of gymnastics.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: So how are you thinking, like-- are you thinking you're definitely going to vote in the Democratic primary? Are you thinking about maybe voting against Trump in the Republican?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm voting against Trump.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Right. So have you thought-- even though Nikki Haley is a little bit-- like, she's got some rough positions on abortion and climate change and all that stuff, have you thought about voting for-- I'm not a Nikki Haley supporter. I'm a left-of-center person. But have you thought about--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, she was the next best candidate until I came here to listen to Dean.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Oh, so--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: So I'm thinking more positively with Dean. Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: So I really like what Dean has to say. And I respect Dean. And if you don't like Biden, I get that that gives you an option. But what I think is--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I just feel he's just too old right now.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Right. But my thinking is, if you're concerned about the threat that Trump brings to our democracy, even though I like Dean more than I like Nikki Haley, like, I think she's a better vote, because he's asking you to damage Biden. And with a vote for Haley, you're damaging Trump.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: And so why vote-- if you're an undeclared voter and you hate Trump and think he's the biggest threat to the country, we need to get-- we need to embarrass Trump here. We need to show Trump losing, and--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: That's a very long hunter circling around some prey to kill. And you're not sure if he took a shot or not, but he thinks this is the best way to talk about Nikki Haley. He has this cautious approach, partially because of this thing people keep saying around here all the time. New Hampshire voters have to make up their own minds. Don't pressure me.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So it can be hard to tell how he's actually doing with this crowd, even though this woman says the most important thing to her is to stop Trump.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But you still don't know what the right path is.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's right. I don't know.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: My pitch would be, if you wanted--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Our whole country feels that way. We just don't know.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: My pitch-- I mean, I come from Maryland. And it's your decision, not mine. But my pitch would be, if you want to stop Trump, you got to vote against the guy, even if it's for somebody you don't like.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I know.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And with that, the voter has to go. We move on. This strategy-- getting people to hate-vote for Nikki Haley-- there's a word some people use for this kind of thing, a technical term in politics for sneaking around and doing dirty tricks inside the other party's election. Here's Ken.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: Someone tweeted that this is the most organized ratfucking operation of all time. Are you familiar with that term?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yes, I am. About you guys?

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. But we don't see ourselves as ratfuckers.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Well, did you feel-- was it a compliment?

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: I believe it was a compliment, yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I think it is.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This whole quest of Robert and Ken's began one night last summer. They met up in DC and got onto the subject of how they think Trump is an existential threat to democracy, and can we get off the road to autocracy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Ken was like, you know, you have done stuff in the past to help other countries in this situation. Maybe we should actually do something.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Ken, I think, given his consulting background, was like, let's do a brainstorm, and this is how you do a brainstorm.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: Yeah, Robert rolled his eyes.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Yeah, well, can I tell her about your other idea that weekend? Ken has some really good ideas and some not so really good ideas. And so the other idea he tried to pitch me on that weekend was that the National Football League is too dangerous, and so we need to have--

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: We just lost half of America.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: It's fine. So let's create a seven-on-seven football league that is more safe, and--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Robert told him that was ridiculous. And here's the sort of person Ken is.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: And then he pulls out a PowerPoint showing his, like, idea for a seven-on-seven football league. And I was like, this is giving me serious doubts that we should proceed along this front. But he still actually believes it's a good idea.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: I do. I do.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So anyway, after they got this idea for defeating Trump, they went out and raised money. And they say they raised $20,000 on their own, and then they got this big chunk of $650,000 from donors who wish to remain anonymous. And that's real money. That could have an impact on a small but mighty election like this one.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: With that money, they bought targeted voter lists of undeclared left-leaning voters that they regularly message and send mailers out to-- mailers and messages that Ken has gotten focus-grouped and tested with professionals. They got a lucky break when Nikki Haley started to poll within 10 points of Donald Trump in New Hampshire. And so right at this moment, going into the Iowa caucus, their hope is she'd come in second in Iowa, that would give her the momentum to win New Hampshire outright, beat Trump, which would make her credible in South Carolina, and beyond that. They even hired two people in South Carolina, in case they have a shot there.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: We always saw this as high risk, high reward. Like, if you looked at the polls, it has always looked like Trump will win the nomination. But if there's a 5% chance of stopping a potential dictator, it's worth putting a lot of effort into that.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Yeah, for that 5% chance that Haley shocks Trump here and there's an alternative in the-- like, it's worth it for our democracy.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Robert is really emotionally invested in this idea-- that maybe they, these two college friends, could actually do something to stop Donald Trump. He's intense about his work always, gets overly invested, it seems. At his day job, he was waking up having panic attacks about that work on top of this work. I was like, is this work helping?

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: No, this is not extremely healthy either. I tied myself into my career. And then rather than seek balance and view myself as a father and a brother and a son-- and instead of that, I have now identified myself as a part of this mission. And I'm wrapped up in that, and my whole self-worth is going to be determined on January 23, and that's not healthy at all.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: So I'm really worried, from a mental health and all that perspective of, like, what happens after January 23 or what happens after the election in November. Like, at some point, there's going to be a reckoning, and I'm really afraid of that, to be honest.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Robert's not alone, of course. They're not the only anti-Trump group trying to sway undeclared voters. And they're not big players, but they're real players. Still, they can go from sophisticated to bumbling very quickly, like when we found ourselves screeching around Manchester in a car on a way to an MLK Day celebration, late.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: As usual, they were glomming on to someone else's event, hoping to meet people who know more people who might carry their message out to other New Hampshirans. They volunteered to bring the coffee and the drinks. Their friend, Moises, was supposed to do it, but he's stuck at UPS printing up flyers with a QR code. The event has already started. Robert's freaking out.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: So we're right by there. So we're going to stop there. You to get to the event and do damage control. Please. They're upset with us.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Get to the event.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: I'm trying. OK, bye.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Robert thinks of himself as responsible. And when he's not seen that way, it kills him.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Because we're going to be five minutes-- 10 minutes late to an MLK event. It's just embarrassing in some ways.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: How's your shame spiral?

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Shame spiral is not in a good place right now.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: When they get there, Robert jumps out with three boxes of coffee, two huge bags of creamers. He's running around in the cold. Can't even find the door.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Can you call Moises and ask how to get in the freaking building? Why don't they have signs? Thank you. Come on, Moises. Answer the phone. Did he not pick up? I'm just really frustrated.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Once they're in, it's apologies and taping their QR code flyers onto Dunkin' Donuts boxes. And Robert works the line of people, tabling for various social justice-y causes, mostly white activists. New Hampshire is mostly white. Ken and Robert are white.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And I get to witness just how tired people are of this kind of pitch. This is the third anybody-but-Trump election. You know what I mean? He talks with Deb Opramolla, who's Black.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: Trump is not sophisticated enough to hide his white supremacy.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Right, and Nikki Haley is more sophisticated at it.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: And she's more-- and the sad thing is, she's a Brown woman--

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: --lifting up white supremacy. So she's just a more sophisticated Trump.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Well, but she also condemned-- she said January 6 was a terrible day, right? She doesn't call her military veterans suckers and losers. Like, would she launch a coup against our country?

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: But she would pardon Trump.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Well, would you rather-- like, would you rather vote for the criminal or the one who pardons the criminal?

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: I would prefer not to vote for either.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Well, right. I get that. But then who are-- you only have one vote in the primaries. And so the question is, like, where can you-- yes, you'd prefer not to vote for either, but then are you just throwing away your vote and letting Trump win?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I saw this move a few times from Robert, talking about people's vote like it was a commodity, like it was just a piece of currency that you could spend at this store or that store, and you just needed to squeeze the most value out of it that you could. That's a hard sell in New Hampshire. And he doesn't always seem so tuned in to how people might be thinking about their vote as theirs-- something between a personal statement and a moral obligation.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: And here's the problem with what you're saying to me, is throwing away my vote--

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: --right-- is that Nikki Haley has yet, really, to address any Blacks. She has not gone out of her way.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Yeah, that's true.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: And when the racism question came up in a very actually simple question to answer, she ran.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: She gave a horrible answer.

segments.speaker: Deb Opramolla
segments.text: No, she ran. My vote is sacred. Am I going to spend it on her? No.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Well, there's one person who will tell you what they're doing-- or what they're not doing.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The Iowa caucuses were that night, Monday. We watched early returns in a bar. Again, Robert was really rooting for Nikki Haley to come in second after Trump, turn the primaries into a two-person race. That's not what happened.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: She came in third, just behind DeSantis and well behind Trump. It's a huge setback, and Robert's upset. Things feel like they're starting to slip away, and he spends the rest of the night scrolling and angrily tweeting.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The next day, they have to regroup. The text messages they'd been planning to send to the 80,000 voters they're targeting were built around Nikki Haley doing better in Iowa. Now, they have to reframe things to make Iowa seem less important.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Ken suggests a stock photo of a guy scratching his head with the words, "Does anyone actually know what a caucus is? New Hampshire picks presidents." Robert points out that he's butchering a famous New Hampshire saying, and they're both so stressed out, here's how that conversation goes down.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: The line that everyone here recognizes, the political line that shows we're plugged into New Hampshire, is that line. "Iowa picks corn. New Hampshire picks presidents." That's the line--

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: --New Hampshire picks presidents.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Yeah, but you're changing-- Iowa has a caucus. Who's ever heard of a caucus? It's not a good line. I'm sorry. I don't like it.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: It's relatable.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: It's the famous line. It's John Sununu's line. There's a history of it. People recognize it.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: Yeah, it's like a cliché here.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Yeah, so?

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: It's not attention grabbing.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Ken, I'm the one that's been in New Hampshire for three months. I understand how the elites are viewing this. I'm telling you that's the line that people know. They don't want to say, what's a caucus.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: Give me credit for being here for three months and talking to every freaking person that I can. That's the line that people-- OK, I'm just saying, the first thing the guy said at the meeting today was that line.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Robert wins out. They go with the famous line and a photo of a cornfield that Robert insisted is provocative. He told Ken--

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: That's why I want to have the cornfields, but you don't want to have that. Like, it's edgy. It's insulting to Iowa.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I met my last voters in New Hampshire later that day. Robert brought me to meet this couple in a lovely house on a snowy street in Manchester. He wanted to run the cornfield text messages by George Bruno, former Democratic Party chair.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: George had volunteered to be a public champion of Robert's cause, and Robert had managed to convince this august New Hampshiran to publicly change his party registration from Democrat to Undeclared. Only problem was, George still hadn't decided if he'll actually do the thing Robert was asking-- vote for Nikki Haley.

segments.speaker: George Bruno
segments.text: I haven't decided.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But it could-- even if--

segments.speaker: George Bruno
segments.text: I think I made that clear. I am undeclared and undecided.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: I've been working on him for five months.

segments.speaker: George Bruno
segments.text: And it will become more clear as we get closer to February 23.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: No, January 23. Don't miss--

segments.speaker: George Bruno
segments.text: Excuse me. January 23.

segments.speaker: George Bruno
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I found this to be an ominous tale for Robert's quixotic mission, if George Bruno, this advocate for Robert's cause, couldn't even commit to doing the thing-- crossing parties, voting to save America in the Republican primary. But then, Robert turned to George's wife, Rona, who'd been in the kitchen while we'd been talking-- offering tea and reading The New York Times. She'd changed her party registration to undeclared, too.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Robert asked her what she was thinking. She said she'd never vote for someone who didn't believe in reproductive rights. Robert said, even though Trump killed off Roe versus Wade? She said, well, that's a good point, actually.

segments.speaker: Rona
segments.text: No, my original intent in crossing over was to assure that Trump would not become president.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Rona
segments.text: Very near and dear to my values is the ability for women to control their own bodies and their reproductive rights. So it would be hard for me to cast a vote for somebody who might not respect that. On the other hand, the most important thing is to assure that he is not the candidate and not president.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You're still--

segments.speaker: Rona
segments.text: So I might have to compromise.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Would you vote for Nikki Haley? She's the one that, according to the polls, looks the most likely to beat Trump.

segments.speaker: Rona
segments.text: Right. Recently, I read some of her stances, and she was really waffling on reproductive rights. So it scared me. On the other hand, I did this primarily to defeat Trump. So if it meant voting for her, I might do it. And I have a little more time to decide.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Your face is just all screwed up.

segments.speaker: Rona
segments.text: It's just because it's such an uncomfortable thought. But I want to defeat Trump. And if it takes voting for Nikki Haley to do that, I think I might do that.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You know, I think she might really do it. When I left New Hampshire, it was halfway through America's magical eight-day period between Iowa's caucuses and New Hampshire's primaries. Robert seemed to swing from happily cherrypicking polls that told him what he wanted to hear to despair and real fear that they had no chance and Trump couldn't be stopped by anyone.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He told me he woke up crying on Thursday morning. This might all be over in a few days, he said-- the Alamo. Their project was a long shot from the start. They did their best. And now, since Trump's overwhelming win in Iowa, it'd gotten way long shottier. So was it worth it?

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: If Trump wins by 15 or 20 points, I will view everything we've done as a failure. And I will consider myself a failure. And I know that's not-- like, we're doing everything we can, and it's not. And I need to be-- like, they tell you you have to be nicer to yourself and speak to you like a friend might speak to you.

segments.speaker: Robert Schwartz
segments.text: And a friend would say, nice try, good job, way to go, way to fight for it anyway. But I will look at-- like, I've made all these sacrifices on this gamble. And if the gamble turned out to be a wrong gamble and our country's not up to stopping Trump, then I made a huge miscalculation.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So that's Roberts anxiety. Here's Ken's.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Do you feel like this is a referendum on yourself, too?

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: I don't.

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ken Scheffler
segments.text: No. I just really want Donald Trump to lose.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: There are 343,192 undeclared voters in New Hampshire. Robert and Ken had just a few more days left to catch some of them, tell them to vote against everything they care about, and hold back, for just a little longer, what appears to be the inevitable course of history.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Zoe Chace is a producer on our show. Coming up, a baby gets in trouble with the law. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's show-- "Embrace The Suck." Apparently, that phrase started in the military and then moved into more general use, meaning you should just own how bad it is. Put your arms around it. Hold it close to you. That is the only way you're going to get through it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today, we have stories of people doing exactly that. We have arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two, The Dream Police. It's hard getting a baby to go to sleep. Everybody knows that. And different parents get through it different ways.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Not long ago, one of our producers, Ike Sriskandarajah and his wife Emma were struggling with this with their son Leroy. At 1 and 1/2 years old, Leroy could say a few words, and he was actually able to hold an umbrella and crudely pull off a few of Gene Kelly's moves from Singing in the Rain while it played. I've seen video of this. He wasn't great, but he was amazing for somebody under 2 feet tall wearing a diaper.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Though I have to say, for all that accomplishment, Leroy was still not on a proper sleep schedule-- until his parents embraced the awfulness of the situation they were in and invented something. Here's Ike.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Leroy is the loudest guy I know. I'm pretty soft-spoken, so he didn't get that from me. One thing he did get-- we both really prefer to be awake. But Leroy takes it a little too far.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: When he was about one, I tried to put him down for a nap in his crib. He had bags under his eyes, his eyelids were heavy, and his head was doing that thing where it falls and snaps back. Then I saw him slap himself in the face to stay awake, like a long-haul trucker, fresh out of 5 Hour Energy.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: And it's not just that he would fight sleep. When he did go to sleep, sometimes he'd wake up in absolute terror. But he needs to go to sleep. We all must. And we tried everything.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: At five months, we tried sleep training. It didn't take. At one year, his soon-to-be daycare provider suggested the cry-it-out method, which, depending on what type of parent you are, is either the most efficient way to sleep train or the most barbaric. When they cry, it's your job not to comfort them. Don't go in, even if it sounds really bad, which it did.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: We were a few weeks into this hellish ritual until one summer day. Leroy was looking sleepy, and it was time to attempt the 1:00 PM nap. I carried him to his room, drew the curtains, turned down the lullabies, gave him a fresh diaper, lowered him into his crib-- "Love you, Leroy, see you after your nap"-- and closed the door.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The crying started immediately, and I turned on a timer. For the next 40 minutes, Emma and I were clenched and approaching the upper threshold of our tolerance when she asked, "Can I pick him up?" "Yes, please." She went into his room, and then I heard our doorbell.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I went to answer. And on the other side were two NYPD officers, a man and a woman. The woman asked, "Is that your baby crying?" "Yes." "We're responding to a child endangerment call."

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: My mind was slowly grasping what was happening. Leroy, the loudest guy I know, had been screaming so much that a neighbor called the cops on us. They thought we were abusing Leroy. "We need to do a child welfare check," they said.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I know these checks can turn into investigations. If you're poor, it can escalate fast. And even if you're not, it can be terrifying. Does Leroy have a scratch or a bruise right now? Are there piles of laundry lying around?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: My adrenaline is pumping. And the voice in my head is telling me to say, fuck you, slam the door, and run with Leroy out the back. But don't listen to that voice. We don't have a back door.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I steadied myself. "You really don't need to do that. My wife, she's feeding him right now. He's busy." The male officer countered. "Either we go into his room or you bring him to us. We won't leave until we complete a visual inspection."

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: "OK." I went to Leroy's room and told Emma, "The cops are here. They need to see Leroy." "But I'm breastfeeding." "I told them that." She brought Leroy to the door.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The woman officer asked, "Are you making all that noise?" Leroy was calm in Emma's arms. Emma said, "Sleep training. It's hard." The woman officer nodded. She gave him a little half baby wave and in a sweet voice said, "OK, you need to go to sleep."

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Before they went, I asked, "Hey, just out of curiosity, can you tell me which neighbor called you guys?" "No." "Oh, OK. That makes sense." I started to hate all the neighbors who lived within earshot and didn't make eye contact.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Our sleep-training experiment was over. We were back to laying on the floor next to his crib and trying to tiptoe out of his room when the coast was clear. Often, it was not.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: One night, Leroy passed the point of no return, crying whether I was there or not. And I got scared that the neighbor might call the cops again. Then I heard a police siren going past our apartment, and I thought, I can work with this.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: "Did you hear that?" Leroy stopped crying and listened. "The policeman. He's driving by to check if you're going to sleep, and you're crying so loud, he can hear you."

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Leroy asked, "What will he do?" Now, there are moments in life that feel like they define what kind of parent you are. Would I be the kind of morally bankrupt parent that scares my child to sleep?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I looked sweet Leroy in his big, beautiful, brown eyes and told him, "If the cops come back, they will take us away in different cars." He curled up under his blanket and closed his eyes tight. I left the room, shut the door behind me, held my breath, and waited.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Silence. Incredible. It worked. And? Oh, god, what have I done? I reported the news to Emma. "Oh, no," she said. "He must be so scared."

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: "Do you think I should go tell him they aren't coming?" "I don't know." "OK. Well, let's never talk about this again." The next night, Leroy asked about the policeman. "Is he coming back?"

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I said, "Yes." And Leroy went to sleep. "Emma, I did it again." "Please don't tell me that." "Do you want me to stop?" "I don't know."

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I said, "Well, now, you're complicit." This became our new routine. Warm bath, cold milk. Emma would virtuosically perform all the voices in a stack of books. Then I would take Leroy to bed and threaten state violence. And we'd all go to sleep.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: After a while, it stopped working. He got wise that the police weren't actually coming to our apartment every night, and he started crying again when I would leave. Now, I think it was Shakespeare who once wrote-- and I'm paraphrasing here-- when you find yourself halfway in a river of blood, either way you go, you've got to go through half a river of blood.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So I forged ahead. One night when Leroy was crying, I closed the door behind me, took a deep breath, and banged on his bedroom door.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: [BANGING]

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: "It's the police. Go to sleep." Just cancel me now. And yeah, it worked. We were living in an imaginary police state for what I'm sure child psychologists would agree was too long. Then one night, Leroy asked me a question I didn't see coming.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: "Will the policeman take my nightmares away?" Take his nightmares away? Not him? Somehow, in Leroy's cool, weird mind, he figured out that if the policeman was so scary, he could also scare whatever was haunting his dreams.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I was stunned. "Of course," I said. "He will take your nightmares. He'll put them in the back of his squad car and take them to jail." Leroy had taken his fear and morphed it into something that could protect him.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I tried to teach Leroy how to sleep and pass along a healthy fear of the police. He learned neither. Leroy's three now. Our bedtime routine is less violent. I lay down next to him in his big-kid bed until he's asleep. The plan is to do this until he turns 18.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: OK. So what do we do at night?

segments.speaker: Leroy
segments.text: Take a soapy bath and put on your pajamas when you're done. Pee in the potty, lotion up, and read a book, and go to bed.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That's it?

segments.speaker: Leroy
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That sounds easy. You just go to bed, no problem.

segments.speaker: Leroy
segments.text: We do all that stuff.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Oh, you forgot one thing.

segments.speaker: Leroy
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: You got to give a hug and a kiss.

segments.speaker: Leroy
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Hug. Hug.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: OK. That's a lick.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ike Sriskandarajah is a producer on our show, currently on parental leave with a new baby who sleeps and wakes at will on his own schedule.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Notes On Cycling. So we end today's show with one last story about things coming apart and somebody who just accepts it and, in fact, embraces it. This comes from Boen Wang, who made this story as a student for a podcasting class he was taking. He recorded his voice tracks into his iPhone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I have to say, I really loved Boen's work whenever I have heard it, because I feel like he is inventing a way to make radio stories that just have their own sort of feeling and sound. Anyway, here he is.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: Don't worry. There's no point.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [WINDOW OPENING]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: In the summer of 2015, I bought a bike from a guy on Craigslist. The bike was $40, so it was shitty. So it suited me.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: I met the guy outside his house. A woman, who was possibly his wife, hung around and made occasional interjections, which he seemed experienced in ignoring. I asked if I could try the bike before I bought it.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: "Let's see the money first," he said. His words were kind of slurred, and his balance was kind of wobbly. His possible wife told him to cut me a break, which he ignored.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: "I just don't want you getting any ideas," he said. So I gave him my backpack as a sort of security deposit, rode in a circle, got off, gave him the money, got my backpack, and rode away. It was downhill from there.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [WINDOW CLOSING]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: Like video games and birding and heroin, people who are into cycling are really into cycling. As for me, I wasn't into anything. I was living in State College, Pennsylvania, and attending Penn State. I lived off campus, so on weekdays, I rode to school, and on weekends, I rode around aimlessly.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: I was changing my major from engineering to English. But I still remembered that total mechanical energy is equal to the sum of kinetic and potential energy. Now that I had no use for this information, I realized that it's actually quite useful that you have to take into account how fast you're going as well as how much faster you can go.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [WIND BLOWING]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: The church I went to held monthly volunteer projects, usually at places far from campus. I never went before, because I didn't know anyone who would give me a ride. But now that I had a bike, I signed up.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: One month, we painted a guy's house. His name was Tony, and he sat at the kitchen table and chain smoked as we painted the walls. During a break, I chatted with him. He told me he had bronchitis, and I avoided pointing out the obvious.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: The next month, I cleaned out a dead woman's house. She had died of cancer. One of the volunteers there, Brian, said she lived alone and didn't have many friends. Her kids didn't call, so she would call Brian at midnight, and she wouldn't stop talking till 4:00 in the morning.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: He didn't seem too torn up about her death. Brian told me he did IT for Penn State. He went to school here in the '80s and stuck around for a few decades. He was her only friend, if you could call him that.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [RECORD NEEDLE]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [DIRTY BEACHES, "LORD KNOWS BEST"]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: There's a video game called Gone Home, where you wander around your family's empty house. It's dark and thundering outside, and you go from room to room, turning on the lights and looking at different objects-- notes on the fridge, your sister's old journal, your mother's weekly salon receipt. The stuff is scattered about seemingly at random, but it's actually arranged in such a way so that a story emerges about the people who live there-- how your parents met and married and had kids and then drifted apart, how your dad may have been molested as a child, how your sister fell in love and ran away.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [MUSIC CUTS]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: The women's house had no story, because life is not a story. Life is boxes filled with yellowed magazines, empty printers, broken CRTs, stereo sets, couches, mattresses, chairs, sheets, lamps, a mountain of material with no throughline. We started with the home office. It overlooked a dumpster in the driveway, so we threw stuff out the window.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [WINDOW OPENING]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: A girl from Germany helped me defenestrate.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: She was a high schooler who, through some sort of exchange program, interned at the church.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: I asked her what sort of responsibilities a church intern had. And she either didn't understand the question or chose to ignore it, and I didn't press the issue.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: The hard part was the furniture. Brian and I tackled the heavy stuff-- the drawers and dressers and cabinets.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: The dumpster was overflowing, so we had to break down the furniture before lifting it up and tipping it in. I felt a childlike satisfaction, turning the detritus of the stranger's life into ever-smaller bits of torn wood and popped nails. Towards the end of the day, Brian and I moved two redwood bookshelves onto the lawn. We'd thrown out the books beforehand. He brought hammers.

segments.speaker: Text-to-speech
segments.text: Instructions for smashing a redwood bookshelf on a dead woman's lawn. One, stand back. Hold the hammer at your hip. Two, move forward at a moderate speed, somewhere between walking and running.

segments.speaker: Text-to-speech
segments.text: (SUBJECT) TEXT-TO-SPEECH, BOEN WANG: Three, make a sweeping motion with your arm, lifting the hammer directly above your head. Four--

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: Impact.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [CICADAS]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: (SUBJECT) TEXT-TO-SPEECH, BOEN WANG: Repeat steps one through four until complete. Ignore the church intern looking at you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At the end of the summer, I lost my best friend. "Lost" isn't the right word to use, as it implies passivity on my part. "Broke up" is closer, except that seems to only apply to romantic relationships. "Pushed away my best friend," "rejected her"-- something like that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I spent the summer biking to her apartment downtown. I told her about the chain smoker and the dead woman and the weird scent of loneliness in their houses. We cooked dinner, played board games, watched movies. We did the things we always did, except now I didn't want to do them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I told her that I didn't like spending time with her, that I didn't like her, that I didn't want to be her friend, that it wasn't her fault but mine, that I didn't understand it either, that I continued doing the things I did because I didn't know what else to do, and that, therefore, I should stop, and therefore we should stop being friends. It struck me even then as a pretty shitty explanation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Most of this came out in a conversation we had walking back to the house I was living at. My bike, going tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, as I felt it twist in my chest, like I was hiding a terrible secret, except when I revealed it, my heart twisted tighter. A few days later, she sent me a 988-word Facebook message, an excerpt of which read--

segments.speaker: Friend
segments.text: If things are bad, can you just ask for a break instead of saying, "I don't want to be friends anymore"? And if you actually don't want to try anymore and you're certain want to let this go, then you can decide to break up. But it's literally the most hurtful thing you can do when you do that.

segments.speaker: Friend
segments.text: So only do it when you've really truly decided that you want to let me go. And I will let go, which doesn't mean that I'll stop loving you or caring about you or praying for you. But in the end, I'll grow to be OK with not having you be a part of my life. You are more important than this relationship.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: I sent her a two-word response. "OK. Sure." Before the school year started, I saw her one more time. She told me that I didn't mean what I was doing, that self-loathing was warping my thinking, that pushing her away seemed like the right thing to do now but wouldn't solve anything.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: In retrospect, it was my last chance.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [STOPWATCH STARTING]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: She folded a piece of paper into a five-pointed star. She'd been in a church retreat the previous weekend and told me an illustration she heard about queer youths who come out in the church.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: When they start out, they have their family, friends, classmates, acquaintances, and the church. She pointed to a star's point for each category. When they come out in a conservative Christian setting, they usually lose their family first, she said, ripping off a piece of the star.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: She went through every category, tearing the star apart piece by piece, until all that was left was a jagged pentagon.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [STOPWATCH STOPPING]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: I don't remember if I said anything. I left and didn't see her for a year.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [RECORD NEEDLE]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: Let me tell you the point.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: [FRANCOISE HARDY, "VOILA"]

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: These days, the brakes on my bike don't work, so I scrape my foot against the ground to stop. When I lie in bed, I think of near misses I've had, cruising down a long hill and almost hurtling into traffic, pressing back with both feet in a desperate attempt to stop. This keeps me up at night, among other things.

segments.speaker: Boen Wang
segments.text: The sole of my shoe is worn down, the rubber layers scraped away, and there's a smooth, gray surface beneath the hard, black sole. One of these days, I'll get the brakes fixed. But for now, I use my foot. Eventually, I stop.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Boen Wang-- he's a writer and audio producer in Pittsburgh. The other voice you heard during the story was Grace Gilbert. To hear more of Boen's work, visit his website, boen.cool. That's B-O-E-N, dot cool.

People who put together today's show include Jendayi Bonds, Sean Cole, Michael Comite, Emmanuel Dzotsi, Stowe Nelson, Katherine Rae Mondo, Nadia Reiman, Safiyah Riddle, Ryan Rumery, Frances Swanson, Kyla Jones, Christopher Swetala, Matt Tierney, Julie Whitaker, and Diane Wu.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our managing editor is Sarah Abdurrahman. Our senior editor is David Kestenbaum. Our executive editor is Emanuele Berry. This is our last show with our fellow, James Bennett the Second.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He is off to a job as one of the hosts of a podcast and radio show at GBH Boston called The Culture Show. We all wish him the best. Special thanks today to Isaac Arnsdorf, James Pindell, Michael Graham, Katherine Dunn, and David Barbeau.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our website, thisamericanlife.org, where you can listen to our archive of over 800 episodes for absolutely free. This American Life is delivered to public radio stations by PRX, the Public Radio Exchange. Thanks, as always, to our program's confounder, Mr. Torey Malatia. He's the king of boggle. There is none higher.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But he hates that little hourglass thingy. When the time starts running out, he always says--

segments.speaker: Kendra
segments.text: Oh, hell, no, you are not going to ruin my day, sand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did I mention how many points he got for "quagmire"? I'm Ira Glass. Back next week with more stories of This American Life.
